# Week 6 Mini-Studio

This page follows the same sequence as [week6-code.R](week6-code.R). It is designed as a stable seminar companion: read the code, run the matching block in R or RStudio, then answer the short prompts here in words. That keeps the focus on the class code, which is the style you are most likely to meet in the exam.

::: {.callout-tip}
## How to use this page

1. Open [week6-code.R](week6-code.R) beside this page.
2. Work through the sections in order.
3. Run the matching block in RStudio.
4. Use the prompts here to practise explanation and model choice, not just syntax.
:::

## A. Build the `holidays` series

This opening block creates the tourism series used in the first half of the seminar.

```r
holidays <- tourism |>
  filter(State %in% c("Victoria", "Queensland")) |>
  filter(Purpose == "Holiday") |>
  as_tibble() |>
  summarise(Trips = sum(Trips), .by = c("State", "Quarter")) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Quarter, key = State)

holidays |>
  autoplot()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- Compare the overall level of Victoria and Queensland.
- Look at whether the seasonal swings stay roughly constant or get larger when the series level gets larger.
- Keep that visual impression in mind before fitting any ETS models.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Exam-style prompt

Before fitting anything, which series looks more likely to need multiplicative seasonality, and why?
:::

## B. Fit competing ETS models

This is the core model comparison block from the seminar. The point is not just to run `ETS()`, but to compare several reasonable choices.

```r
fit <- holidays |>
  model(
    additive = ETS(Trips ~ error("A")),
    multiplicative = ETS(Trips ~ error("M")),
    auto = ETS(Trips)
  )

fit
fit |>
  glance()
```

```r
fit |>
  filter(State == "Victoria") |>
  select(multiplicative) |>
  report()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- `glance()` is the quick comparison table.
- `report()` tells you the actual selected structure and smoothing parameters.
- The important habit is to connect the formal model output back to the visual behaviour of the series.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Exam-style prompt

For Victoria, which model looks most appropriate? Use evidence from both `glance()` and `report()`, not just one or the other.
:::

## C. Check components and residuals

Good model choice is not just about a criterion value. You also need to inspect what the fitted model is doing and whether the residuals look reasonable.

```r
fit |>
  filter(State == "Victoria") |>
  select(multiplicative) |>
  components() |>
  autoplot()
```

```r
fit |>
  filter(State == "Victoria") |>
  select(multiplicative) |>
  gg_tsresiduals()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Try this

Change `State == "Victoria"` to `State == "Queensland"` and compare the outputs.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- In the components plot, ask what trend and seasonal pattern the model is trying to capture.
- In the residual diagnostics, ask whether there is still obvious structure left behind.
- You do not need perfect residuals to say something useful, but you should be able to explain whether the model seems adequate.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Exam-style prompt

How would you justify the Victoria model in words after checking both the fitted components and the residual diagnostics?
:::

## D. Forecast and defend the model choice

This section turns model choice into forecast interpretation, which is much closer to exam reasoning than simply listing the chosen ETS form.

```r
fc <- fit |>
  forecast()

fc |>
  autoplot(holidays) +
  labs(title = "Overnight trips (thousands)")
```

```r
fc |>
  filter(State == "Victoria", !.model == "auto") |>
  autoplot(holidays) +
  labs(title = "Victoria: Overnight trips (thousands)") +
  facet_wrap(vars(.model), ncol = 1)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- Compare the shape of the forecasts, not just the labels.
- Ask whether the amplitude of the seasonal pattern scales with the level.
- That scaling idea is the main reason multiplicative seasonality becomes attractive here.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Exam-style prompt

Write two or three sentences answering this question: why is the multiplicative model needed for Victoria?
:::

## E. Build and inspect `h02`

The seminar then switches to the `PBS` example. This is a fresh model-choice problem, so start again from the series features.

```r
h02 <- PBS |>
  filter(ATC2 == "H02") |>
  summarise(Cost = sum(Cost))

h02 |>
  autoplot(Cost)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- Look for trend.
- Look for seasonality.
- Look for whether the variation changes with the level.
- Try to predict the sort of ETS structure you expect before asking the software.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Exam-style prompt

Based on the time plot alone, what ETS features look plausible for `h02`?
:::

## F. Auto ETS and damped trend

Now compare what automatic ETS suggests with a more deliberate trend choice.

```r
h02 |>
  model(ETS(Cost)) |>
  report()
```

```r
h02 |>
  model(ETS(Cost ~ trend("A"))) |>
  forecast(h = "8 years") |>
  autoplot(h02)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Try this

Change `trend("A")` to `trend("Ad")`. Then change `h = "8 years"` to `h = "20 years"`.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- A damped trend matters most when the forecast horizon gets longer.
- The question is not whether the trend exists, but whether it should continue indefinitely at the same rate.
- That is an interpretation question, not just a software question.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Exam-style prompt

Why might a damped trend be more sensible than a plain additive trend for `h02`?
:::

## G. STL plus ETS

The last block combines decomposition and forecasting. This is useful when you want to separate pattern description from the final forecasting step.

```r
h02 |>
  model(STL(Cost)) |>
  components() |>
  autoplot()
```

```r
stl_fit <- h02 |>
  model(
    decomposition_model(
      STL(Cost),
      ETS(season_adjust),
      SNAIVE(season_year)
    )
  )

stl_fit |>
  report()

stl_fit |>
  forecast(h = "20 years") |>
  autoplot(h02)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Try this

Change `STL(Cost)` to `STL(log(Cost) ~ season(window = "periodic"))` and compare how that changes the decomposition story.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- STL helps you think separately about trend, seasonality, and remainder.
- After decomposition, you still have to justify the final forecasting choice.
- The aim is not “use STL because it is fancy”; the aim is to explain when decomposition gives a more sensible forecasting workflow.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Exam-style prompt

When would you prefer an STL plus ETS approach over fitting a single ETS model directly?
:::

## Final Week 6 check

If you revise only three things from Week 6, make them these:

1. Start with the series features before naming a model.
2. Use `glance()`, `report()`, residual checks, and forecast shape together.
3. Explain why a model is sensible in words, not just by quoting the chosen ETS form.

For the full seminar workflow, keep [week6-code.R](week6-code.R) open while you work through this page. For additional worked material, you can also compare with [Week 6 Tutorial Solution.html](Week6.html).
